concept.name: First notice day
concept.definition: The first day on which notices of intent to deliver the actual commodity against open short futures positions can be issued (received by longs); the date varies by commodity and exchange.
concept.intuition: First notice day is when holding a long futures position stops being purely financial: from then on, a long can be handed a delivery notice and be obliged to pay for and take the goods.
concept.mechanics: In physically delivered markets, shorts may tender delivery notices from first notice day through the delivery period; the clearing organization assigns them to longs, who must pay the invoice price. First notice day often falls before the delivery month and before the last trading day, so speculators typically exit or roll long positions beforehand.
concept.failure_modes: Longs who overlook first notice day can be assigned delivery against their will, requiring full contract-value funding and triggering liquidation by brokers who do not support delivery; liquidity also thins as commercials dominate the final sessions.
concept.misconceptions: First notice day is not the same as the last trading day, and it is not uniform across markets — each contract's calendar sets its own, sometimes weeks before trading ends.
concept.example: For many CBOT grain contracts, first notice day is the last business day preceding the delivery month, so a speculator long December corn would normally exit by late November to avoid delivery assignment.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
